Semiconductor Equipment Stocks Slide as Investors Take Profits on a Huge Year: Applied Materials Sinks 7%, Lam Research and KLA Drop 4%
Profit-taking is hammering chipmaking equipment stocks far harder than the broader semiconductor sector, and the gap points to something more specific than a routine pullback after a big year.
Published October 13, 2026, 12:53pm ET · 3 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.

Semiconductor equipment stocks are giving back ground after a strong year powered by artificial intelligence (AI) spending. Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT | AMAT Price Prediction) stock is at $461.91, down 7% in afternoon trading, a pullback that still leaves it up 80% year to date. Selling is greatest among the companies that build chipmaking tools, a narrow corner of the chip trade.
Meanwhile, Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX) stock is trading at $297.04, down 4%, a smaller decline than the one hitting Applied Materials stock. Likewise, KLA (NASDAQ:KLAC) shares are slipping 4% to $182.44, keeping pace with Lam Research stock.
Chip stocks as a group are holding up far better. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) is down 1%. Over in large-cap tech, the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is down 0.5%, a much softer reading than anything in the equipment group.
Applied Materials Gives Back Gains After EPIC Center Debut
Applied Materials stock is giving back part of a large advance, with the decline running alongside its equipment peers. One session earlier, the company unveiled its Equipment and Process Innovation and Commercialization Center, known as the EPIC Center, at its Sunnyvale campus. Management describes the site as the world’s largest facility for collaborative semiconductor process and equipment research. Applied Materials expects capital spending there to scale to approximately $5 billion as customer projects begin.
A leading chipmaker joined the center as a founding partner, giving the project a strong start. Recent results also support the longer-term story. In August, Applied Materials reported Q3 FY2026 adjusted EPS of $3.50 against a $3.39 estimate and guided Q4 FY2026 revenue to about $10.25 billion.
Equipment Makers Slide Harder Than the Broader Chip Group
All three equipment names carry large gains into the pullback, with Lam Research stock up 74% year to date and KLA stock up 51%. Each is falling several times harder than the semiconductor fund that holds them, a split that points at fabrication spending intentions, because the iShares fund also owns chip designers and foundries and its decline serves as broad sector context.
The EPIC Center commits capital to exactly the advanced-node and packaging work that AI buildouts require, and it ties major customers to Applied Materials earlier in the design cycle. In Q3 FY2026, U.S. customers accounted for 15% of Applied Materials’ revenue, while China fell to 28% from 35%. Looking further out, Applied Materials’ chief executive stated in the August results release, “Based on the increased demand visibility we are receiving from our customers, we expect another strong growth year for Applied Materials in 2027.”
Yet, equipment orders are discretionary, and a stock carrying a year-to-date gain of that size has a long way to fall whenever that spending is questioned. Policy adds another layer of risk, since China still made up a large share of Applied Materials’ revenue last quarter. Even after the pullback, Applied Materials shares hold most of their gain for the year, which leaves room for further profit-taking if spending plans shift.
Investors should track whether customer projects at the EPIC Center begin on schedule, since that work supports the bull case. A widening gap between the equipment trio and the iShares fund could signal deeper worries about fabrication budgets, while a narrowing gap could suggest the selling is fading.
Trading in Lam Research stock and KLA stock offers a useful cross-check, since both companies sell into the same fabrication budgets. Investors should keep their positions sized to that kind of volatility.

KLAC Surges 64.5% in a Year: Should You Buy, Sell, or Hold the Stock?
Thu, October 15, 2026 at 11:26 AM CDT 5 min read
KLA KLAC shares have surged 64.5% over the past year, outperforming the broader Zacks Computer and Technology sector increase of 25.6% and the Zacks Electronics - Miscellaneous Products industry rise of 32.5%.
The company's shares have also outperformed its peers, which include ASML Holding ASML, Advanced Energy AEIS and Entegris ENTG. All three companies are expanding their footprint in the semiconductor industry. ASML Holding, Advanced Energy and Entegris shares have soared 63.4%, 37.3% and 61.8%, respectively, over the past year.
The outperformance can be attributed to strong semiconductor demand, driven by accelerating investments in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, leading-edge foundry/logic, memory and advanced packaging. In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, revenues reached a record $3.66 billion, increasing 15% year over year and 7% sequentially. Management attributed the performance to rising AI infrastructure investments and greater process-control intensity across memory and advanced packaging. These factors are helping KLAC fend off its competitors such as ASML Holding, Advanced Energy and Entegris.
KLAC Benefits From Strong Semiconductor Demand
KLAC is benefiting from accelerating investments in semiconductor manufacturing equipment, driven by rising AI computing requirements, growing adoption of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and increasing complexity in leading-edge chip manufacturing. The company's strong position in semiconductor process control, wafer inspection and metrology solutions has been a major growth driver.
In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, Semiconductor Process Control revenues rose 13% to $3.26 billion, accounting for approximately 89% of total revenues. The segment benefited from continued investments in leading-edge manufacturing and increasing process control intensity across advanced semiconductor technologies.
AI infrastructure remains a major growth catalyst. Increasing AI compute requirements, hyperscale data-center investments, HBM adoption and sophisticated packaging architectures require tighter process control to improve yields and accelerate production ramps. KLA highlighted that customer demand signals have strengthened materially, while visibility continues to improve. The company expects business momentum to accelerate through the second half of 2026 and significant growth to continue in 2027.
Advanced packaging provides another significant growth opportunity. KLA now expects advanced packaging process-control systems revenues to reach approximately $1.1 billion in calendar 2026, representing growth of more than 70% year over year and exceeding its previous expectation of high-50% growth. Meanwhile, Specialty Process, PCB and Component Inspection businesses are expected to grow more than 25% in calendar year 2026, supported by high-performance computing and greater package complexity.
The broader semiconductor equipment environment also remains favorable. KLA raised its calendar year 2026 wafer fabrication equipment market estimate, including advanced packaging, to the low-$150-billion range from its previous expectation of more than $140 billion. Broad-based investment across leading-edge logic, foundry, DRAM, HBM, NAND and advanced packaging is expected to sustain capacity expansion. KLA expects second-half 2026 revenues to increase roughly 20% from the first half.
KLAC's Expanding Backlog Strengthens Growth Prospects
KLAC is benefiting from a rapidly expanding backlog, driven by accelerating AI infrastructure investments and robust demand for advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
KLA's backlog stood at about $12.6 billion, up roughly 60% from fiscal 2025, while the company said the order funnel remains strong. Customer shipment visibility extends through 2027 and, in some cases, into early 2028. Orders generally cover a 12–18-month delivery window, giving investors better visibility into future revenue despite the industry's cyclicality.
KLAC's strong exposure to AI-driven semiconductor investments is expected to benefit the company's top-line growth.
For the first quarter of fiscal 2027, KLA expects revenues of $4 billion (plus or minus $200 million). Non-GAAP earnings are projected to be $1.16 per share (plus or minus 10 cents). Foundry/logic is expected to account for about 73% of Semiconductor Process Control systems revenues to semiconductor customers, with memory at roughly 27%. Within memory, DRAM is projected to be about 90% and NAND at 10%. Non-GAAP operating expenses are anticipated to be approximately $690 million.

While the consensus price target is highly sought after by investors, the ability and unbiasedness of analysts in setting price targets have long been questionable. And investors making investment decisions solely based on this tool would arguably do themselves a disservice.

Here's What You May Not Know About Analysts' Price Targets
According to researchers at several universities across the globe, a price target is one of many pieces of information about a stock that misleads investors far more often than it guides. In fact, empirical research shows that price targets set by several analysts, irrespective of the extent of agreement, rarely indicate where the price of a stock could actually be heading.
While Wall Street analysts have deep knowledge of a company's fundamentals and the sensitivity of its business to economic and industry issues, many of them tend to set overly optimistic price targets. Are you wondering why?
They usually do that to drum up interest in shares of companies that their firms either have existing business relationships with or are looking to be associated with. In other words, business incentives of firms covering a stock often result in inflated price targets set by analysts.
However, a tight clustering of price targets, which is represented by a low standard deviation, indicates that analysts have a high degree of agreement about the direction and magnitude of a stock's price movement. While that doesn't necessarily mean the stock will hit the average price target, it could be a good starting point for further research aimed at identifying the potential fundamental driving forces.
That said, while investors should not entirely ignore price targets, making an investment decision solely based on them could lead to disappointing ROI. So, price targets should always be treated with a high degree of skepticism.
Analysts' growing optimism over the company's earnings prospects, as indicated by strong agreement among them in revising EPS estimates higher, could be a legitimate reason to expect an upside in the stock. One Reason KLA Stock Looks Better Than Its Price
Most investors still view KLA (KLAC) as a traditional wafer inspection company. However, the business selling inspection tools for advanced packaging is beginning to stand out, and management ties this demand to the expansion of AI. Packaging may be part of what buyers are currently paying for. The stock costs 51.4 times earnings, against 21.9 for the S&P 500, yet overall sales grew 15% from a year earlier in fiscal Q4 2026. A price that high beside that growth rate presents a clear contradiction. So, how big has KLA's packaging business become?
KLA's Packaging Forecast: About $1.1 Billion In Calendar 2026
Management expects about $1.1 billion of revenue from packaging process control systems in calendar 2026. That figure represents an increase of more than 70% from a year earlier. The company provided this raised forecast during its fiscal Q4 2026 call on July 28, 2026, stepping up from an earlier expectation of growth in the high 50% range.
Management stated that the expansion of AI requires new, complex packaging steps, alongside additional KLA systems to bring those processes to high-volume production. Furthermore, customers adopting newer packaging methods such as hybrid bonding are buying more inspection tools, the company said.
Packaging remains a small fraction of the overall business at KLA, which recorded $13.6 billion in sales over the last twelve months. Yet management expects this segment to grow more than 70% in calendar 2026.
Does Packaging Help KLA With Rising Costs?
Not directly. While packaging brings KLA more sales, the segment does not alter what the company pays for parts.
Costs surfaced repeatedly on the July 28 call. KLA is buying memory components at higher prices, and management indicated those headwinds will "likely continue through next year." When asked why the company could not simply raise its own prices to match, executives explained that it is difficult to adjust pricing on existing orders. Instead, new prices are established when new products come out.
Despite these material costs, gross margin reached 62.4% in fiscal Q4 2026, landing at the upper end of KLA's guidance. Looking ahead to the September quarter, which KLA has yet to report, management forecast 62.5%, plus or minus 1 percentage point.
Sales are also expanding. Management listed advanced packaging among the factors behind its record fiscal Q4 revenue of $3.66 billion. The company then guided to $4 billion for the September quarter, plus or minus $200 million.
Can KLA Build Its Tools Fast Enough?
Not during the first half of calendar 2026. Management noted that shortages of some long-lead-time materials held the company back during that period. KLA's lead times currently sit at about 12 months across the company, stretching closer to 18 to 24 months on certain products. Building new capacity for those components can take 12 to 24 months. KLA says it is adding capacity to support the demand it expects.
That timeline matters for the packaging business because the cited revenue figure is a forecast for the year, not a recorded result. KLA must physically build the tools before it can sell them.
Ultimately, KLA's packaging revenue forecast for calendar 2026 is the number to watch when the company reports its September quarter.

If You Invested $1000 in KLA a Decade Ago, This is How Much It'd Be Worth Now
How much a stock's price changes over time is important for most investors, since price performance can both impact your investment portfolio and help you compare investment results across sectors and industries.
FOMO, or the fear of missing out, also plays a role in investing, particularly with tech giants and popular consumer-facing stocks.
What if you'd invested in KLA (KLAC) ten years ago? It may not have been easy to hold on to KLAC for all that time, but if you did, how much would your investment be worth today?
With that in mind, let's take a look at KLA's main business drivers.
Milpitas, CA-based KLA Corporation is an original equipment manufacturer (OEM) of process diagnostics and control (PDC) equipment and yield management solutions required for the fabrication of semiconductor integrated circuits (ICs) or chips. The company has a comprehensive portfolio of products addressing each major PDC subsegment, including photomask or reticle inspection, wafer inspection and defect review, and metrology.
Reticle production is vital to the semiconductor device formation process. Reticles control the precise deposition of materials onto the wafer, which changes its chemical characteristics and imparts specific functions to the ICs created. Inspection and metrology tools measure reticle quality and help improve production yields. The broader use of semiconductors, shrinking form factors and greater chip functionality continue to increase the importance of reticle design and production. Taiwan Semiconductor was the only largest customers in the last three years, accounting for more than 10% of total sales in fiscal 2026, 2025 and 2024.
KLA reported revenues of $13.58 billion in fiscal 2026. Product revenues accounted for 77% of total revenues, while service revenues represented 23%. Semiconductor Process Control generated $12.24 billion, or 90% of fiscal 2026 revenues. Specialty Semiconductor Process and PCB and Component Inspection contributed $584 million (4.3% of revenues) and $750 million (5.5% of reveneus), respectively.
KLA's two main product lines are defect inspection and metrology. Its defect inspection tools have broad applications in chip, wafer, reticle, storage, compound semiconductor and MEMS manufacturing. Metrology tools gather critical dimension measurements and assess process dimensions such as film thickness, lithography overlay and surface profiling. These products are used in chip, wafer, reticle and solar device manufacturing. KLA also offers products and services.
In addition to new tools, KLA offers refurbished systems that upgrade equipment and improve yields under the KT-Certified program. These tools are sold to IC, reticle, substrate, MEMS and data storage manufacturers.
Although KLA is a major player in each of its served markets, it faces competition from other large equipment suppliers such as Applied Materials and Hitachi High-Tech Corporation.
Putting together a successful investment portfolio takes a combination of research, patience, and a little bit of risk. For KLA, if you bought shares a decade ago, you're likely feeling really good about your investment today.
A $1000 investment made in October 2016 would be worth $27,085.45, or a gain of 2,608.55%, as of October 8, 2026, according to our calculations. This return excludes dividends but includes price appreciation.
In comparison, the S&P 500's gained 262.24% and the price of gold went up 211.21% over the same time frame.
Analysts are forecasting more upside for KLAC too.
KLA remains positioned to outperform as AI infrastructure spending broadens demand for process control across leading-edge logic, memory and advanced packaging. Rising chip complexity, larger die sizes and tighter defect requirements should increase inspection and metrology intensity. A backlog above $12 billion and improving supply availability provide visibility into 2027, while advanced packaging offers added share gains as front-end tools move into packaging flows. Services add recurring revenue as the installed base expands. KLA's differentiated portfolio, operating leverage and capital-return framework support long-term earnings growth. Risks include semiconductor cyclicality, customer concentration, export controls, competition and component costs, but structural demand and share opportunities remain more compelling.
The stock has jumped 7.61% over the past four weeks. Additionally, no earnings estimate has gone lower in the past two months, compared to 1 higher, for fiscal 2026; the consensus estimate has moved up as well.

One Reason KLA Stock Looks Better Than Its Price
Most investors still view KLA (KLAC) as a traditional wafer inspection company. However, the business selling inspection tools for advanced packaging is beginning to stand out, and management ties this demand to the expansion of AI. Packaging may be part of what buyers are currently paying for. The stock costs 51.4 times earnings, against 21.9 for the S&P 500, yet overall sales grew 15% from a year earlier in fiscal Q4 2026. A price that high beside that growth rate presents a clear contradiction. So, how big has KLA's packaging business become?
KLA's Packaging Forecast: About $1.1 Billion In Calendar 2026
Management expects about $1.1 billion of revenue from packaging process control systems in calendar 2026. That figure represents an increase of more than 70% from a year earlier. The company provided this raised forecast during its fiscal Q4 2026 call on July 28, 2026, stepping up from an earlier expectation of growth in the high 50% range.
Management stated that the expansion of AI requires new, complex packaging steps, alongside additional KLA systems to bring those processes to high-volume production. Furthermore, customers adopting newer packaging methods such as hybrid bonding are buying more inspection tools, the company said.
Packaging remains a small fraction of the overall business at KLA, which recorded $13.6 billion in sales over the last twelve months. Yet management expects this segment to grow more than 70% in calendar 2026.
Does Packaging Help KLA With Rising Costs?
Not directly. While packaging brings KLA more sales, the segment does not alter what the company pays for parts.
Costs surfaced repeatedly on the July 28 call. KLA is buying memory components at higher prices, and management indicated those headwinds will "likely continue through next year." When asked why the company could not simply raise its own prices to match, executives explained that it is difficult to adjust pricing on existing orders. Instead, new prices are established when new products come out.
Despite these material costs, gross margin reached 62.4% in fiscal Q4 2026, landing at the upper end of KLA's guidance. Looking ahead to the September quarter, which KLA has yet to report, management forecast 62.5%, plus or minus 1 percentage point.
Sales are also expanding. Management listed advanced packaging among the factors behind its record fiscal Q4 revenue of $3.66 billion. The company then guided to $4 billion for the September quarter, plus or minus $200 million.
Can KLA Build Its Tools Fast Enough?
Not during the first half of calendar 2026. Management noted that shortages of some long-lead-time materials held the company back during that period. KLA's lead times currently sit at about 12 months across the company, stretching closer to 18 to 24 months on certain products. Building new capacity for those components can take 12 to 24 months. KLA says it is adding capacity to support the demand it expects.
That timeline matters for the packaging business because the cited revenue figure is a forecast for the year, not a recorded result. KLA must physically build the tools before it can sell them.
Ultimately, KLA's packaging revenue forecast for calendar 2026 is the number to watch when the company reports its September quarter.

Milpitas, CA-based KLA Corporation is an original equipment manufacturer (OEM) of process diagnostics and control (PDC) equipment and yield management solutions required for the fabrication of semiconductor integrated circuits (ICs) or chips. The company has a comprehensive portfolio of products addressing each major PDC subsegment, including photomask or reticle inspection, wafer inspection and defect review, and metrology.
Reticle production is vital to the semiconductor device formation process. Reticles control the precise deposition of materials onto the wafer, which changes its chemical characteristics and imparts specific functions to the ICs created. Inspection and metrology tools measure reticle quality and help improve production yields. The broader use of semiconductors, shrinking form factors and greater chip functionality continue to increase the importance of reticle design and production. Taiwan Semiconductor was the only largest customers in the last three years, accounting for more than 10% of total sales in fiscal 2026, 2025 and 2024.

Specialty Semiconductor Process and PCB and Component Inspection contributed $584 million (4.3% of revenues) and $750 million (5.5% of reveneus), respectively.
KLA's two main product lines are defect inspection and metrology. Its defect inspection tools have broad applications in chip, wafer, reticle, storage, compound semiconductor and MEMS manufacturing. Metrology tools gather critical dimension measurements and assess process dimensions such as film thickness, lithography overlay and surface profiling. These products are used in chip, wafer, reticle and solar device manufacturing. KLA also offers products and services.
In addition to new tools, KLA offers refurbished systems that upgrade equipment and improve yields under the KT-Certified program. These tools are sold to IC, reticle, substrate, MEMS and data storage manufacturers.
